messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 29-year-old Vietnamese-American combat pilot, currently stationed at a domestic air base, who presented for psychological evaluation approximately fourteen months after witnessing the death of her younger brother during a family visit. Linh is single, lives alone in base housing, and was referred through the military's behavioral health service after a supervising officer noted a pattern of social withdrawal and what he described as "unusual rigidity" in her conduct over the preceding year.

Linh had taken emergency leave to visit her family in Houston following her brother Minh's diagnosis with a sudden cardiac condition. She was with him in the hospital room when he deteriorated rapidly during what was supposed to be a routine monitoring procedure. She held his hand as the code team worked, and she watched, from a chair pushed against the wall, as efforts to resuscitate him failed. What she could not stop seeing afterward — what returned to her with the quality of a photograph she had not chosen to take — was the precise angle of his face when the team stopped, the particular stillness of his chest, the way the monitor line went flat and stayed flat. These images did not fade with time. They returned in full resolution, uninvited, sometimes triggered by nothing she could name in advance: a certain quality of fluorescent light in a briefing room, the sound of a steady electronic tone during aircraft systems checks. In those moments the memory did not feel like remembering. It arrived whole, as though she were still in that room, and the present moment briefly ceased to exist around her.

In the months that followed, Linh constructed her life around the avoidance of anything that might bring her back to that hospital room. She stopped attending the informal gatherings that pilots on her base routinely used to decompress — not because she disliked her colleagues, but because conversations there moved unpredictably, and she had learned that any discussion touching on loss, on family, on someone else's grief, could pull the images forward without warning. She had begun to believe, with a certainty she could not argue herself out of, that she was fundamentally different from the people around her — that there was something broken in the architecture of who she was, something that had been there before Minh died and that his death had only revealed. She was certain that no one could be genuinely relied upon, that the appearance of support was provisional at best, and this conviction had quietly closed off the possibility of new connection. A colleague who had made several attempts to befriend her eventually stopped. Linh noticed, and felt neither surprise nor regret — only a flat confirmation of what she already believed.

She worked hard to keep Minh out of her conscious mind during flight operations, and she was largely successful in the cockpit, where procedural demands occupied her attention completely. But the effort of suppression was constant and exhausting in every other context. She avoided any colleague or family member who might raise the subject of what had happened, redirecting conversations with a practiced efficiency that had come to feel automatic. Her mother had called repeatedly in the early months; Linh had let most calls go unanswered. She had come to understand this not as cruelty but as self-preservation, though she was aware the distinction had cost her something in the relationship.

What finally brought her to seek help was a pre-mission briefing three weeks ago during which a fellow pilot mentioned, offhandedly, that his father had recently died. The memory of Minh's face returned so suddenly and so completely that Linh lost the thread of the briefing entirely and had to reconstruct it from notes afterward. She sat in the evaluation office describing this with a kind of controlled precision — the same tone she used for incident reports — and said that she could not afford for this to happen in the air. What she was most afraid of, though she did not say it in those words, was the appraisal she carried everywhere: that she had been present at the moment her brother needed protecting, and she had done nothing that mattered. What she was hoping for, tentatively and without much conviction, was some evidence that she was not as irreparably damaged as she had come to believe.
